sources.entry: SQL should be the default choice for data transformation logic

summary.title: SQL should be the default choice for data transformation logic
summary.one_liner: SQL is argued to be the first option for data engineering transformation work because it is readable, durable, testable, and increasingly fast, with DuckDB, CTEs and SQLGlot helping it meet good engineering practice.
takeaways: SQL is declarative, widely understood across roles, and has remained stable for decades, so pipelines written in it age well.
DuckDB, CTEs and SQLGlot make SQL easier to unit test, iterate on, and align with software engineering practice.
SQL engines are strongly typed and Apache Arrow helps with cross-tool data type consistency, reducing typing headaches.
SQL is less suitable where a single pandas call (e.g. resample for time series interpolation) or graph-like data is involved; a presumption against other tools needs strong justification.
Splink is an example: its core computations are in SQL as step-by-step CTEs, running on DuckDB, SQLite, Spark or Athena.
summary.summary: The author argues that SQL should be the first option considered for new data engineering work, citing readability by a wide audience, stability over decades, automatic speed gains from modern engines like DuckDB and distributed Spark/Presto, and fewer dependency maintenance burdens. He says modern tools (DuckDB for zero-dependency unit tests, CTEs for splitting queries into testable parts, SQLGlot for dialect translation) address older criticisms. The post also covers cases where other tools may be preferable, uses his Splink record linkage library as a case study of an SQL-based design, and closes with trends such as compile-to-SQL APIs (Ibis, Malloy, dbplyr) and dbt.
